claims.text: Conventional carbon steels used in chemical processing typically contain non-metallic inclusions and microstructural segregation.
Vacuum arc remelting significantly reduces non-metallic inclusions in carbon steel relative to conventional melting.
Vacuum arc remelting significantly reduces compositional segregation in carbon steel relative to conventional melting.
Two sample sets should be prepared using VAR and conventional melting, respectively.
The two sample sets should be tested under identical mildly acidic chloride conditions at ambient temperature.
SEM, TEM, and EDS can be used to quantify inclusion density and assess other microstructural variables.
Non-metallic inclusions and segregated impurity stringers can act as local anodic or cathodic sites in conventionally processed carbon steel.
Non-metallic inclusions initiate localized corrosion by disrupting passive-film formation.
Reducing non-metallic inclusions through VAR produces a more homogeneous and protective passive film.
A more homogeneous and protective passive film increases the corrosion resistance of carbon steel under mildly acidic chloride conditions.
VAR-processed steel will have lower corrosion current density than conventionally processed steel.
VAR-processed steel will exhibit fewer localized pits than conventionally processed steel.
VAR-processed steel will exhibit a more uniform passive film than conventionally processed steel.
Conventionally melted carbon steel has higher inclusion density, less-uniform passive films, and more localized corrosion than VAR-processed steel under the same test conditions.
The hypothesized relationship is expected to hold for carbon steels in mildly acidic chloride environments at ambient temperature.
Compositional segregation and secondary-phase formation may independently affect corrosion performance.
Failure to observe statistically significant reductions in corrosion current density and pitting density in the VAR samples would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of VAR processing to produce a significant difference in inclusion density would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The intervention is intended to reduce both inclusions and compositional segregation, while the study also seeks to hold other microstructural factors constant and acknowledges segregation as an alternative cause. Co-varying segregation with inclusion density prevents the experiment from cleanly attributing corrosion changes to inclusions alone.

The falsification rule treats finding no significant reduction in inclusion density as falsification, but that result would show failure to implement the proposed mediator rather than refute the claimed causal effect of reduced inclusions.
